surveyDefinition.title: Running Shoes — consumer survey (U.S.)
surveyDefinition.studyPurpose: Identify which of 4 behavioural segments each respondent belongs to, based on running frequency, purchase drivers, price sensitivity, and sustainability orientation.

segments.name: High-Frequency Performance Runners
segments.description: Run multiple times per week, prioritize cushioning, support, and durability, willing to pay premium for performance, replace shoes every 3-6 months.

segments.name: Price-Sensitive Recreational Runners
segments.description: Run occasionally (1-2 times per week) or for fitness, highly price-conscious, often buy on sale or from discount retailers, value durability and comfort but not willing to pay premium.

segments.name: Eco-Conscious Committed Runners
segments.description: Run regularly and are strongly motivated by sustainability, seek recycled materials and carbon-neutral options, willing to pay more for eco-friendly products, but also expect performance.

segments.name: Comfort-Led Casual Users
segments.description: Use running shoes for walking, casual wear, or light jogging, prioritize fit and comfort above all, often have foot issues (arch support), less frequent runners, moderate price sensitivity.

surveyDefinition.whatThisSurveyIs: A segmentation study of Running Shoes buyers in U.S.. It asks how people use Running Shoes, how they choose it, and what would make them switch — then sorts respondents into the behavioural groups defined below. Questions stay at category level: no named brands, and nothing about adjacent categories.
surveyDefinition.whoseContextThisIs: Adults in U.S. who buy or use Running Shoes for personal or household use. Respondents qualify if they: Individuals who have bought running shoes in the past 12 months; Individuals who run or exercise regularly (at least once a week); Individuals who are the primary decision-maker for their own shoe purchase. Excluded: Professional athletes whose shoes are provided by sponsors; Businesses purchasing shoes for employees or resale; Children under 18 (unless purchasing for themselves, but typically parent decides).
surveyDefinition.whyTheseRespondents: Everyday consumers buy running shoes for personal use, pay for them out of pocket, and decide which pair to purchase based on fit, style, and performance. While some businesses may purchase shoes for employees (e.g., athletic teams), the dominant and defining buyer is the individual consumer.
respondentBehaviours: Engages in running or jogging at least occasionally
Purchases athletic footwear for fitness, sport, or casual wear
Researches brands, reviews, and features before buying
May be brand loyal or open to switching based on price/performance
whatIsDeliberatelyNotAsked: Age or household income as behavioural questions — no finding in this survey is driven by them. They are asked once, at the end, in Profiling, and used only to cross-tabulate the behavioural results.
Brand, company or manufacturer names — the survey stays at category level so findings are not tied to one competitor set.
Where the respondent lives — region is chosen when viewing the results, so asking it again would waste a question.
surveyDefinition.howToReadTheNumbers: Percentages are modelled estimates built from published market evidence — they are not measurements from fielded interviews, and should be read as an expected shape of response rather than a result. Single-choice, ranking and rating-scale questions sum to 100%. Multi-select questions do not — each option is an independent share of respondents choosing it. The N shown on each question is the display base for that item.

structure.storyline: Questions run in a planned narrative order: broad and easy first, specific and sensitive last.
structure.storylineSummary: The survey opens by establishing the respondent's running frequency and context, then moves to their shoe ownership and replacement habits, and finally their fit experience. It then traces the purchase journey from trigger through research, channel, and price, ending with the decision drivers. Next, it explores their must-have features, quality cues, sustainability expectations, and trade-offs, closing with value perception. Finally, it measures satisfaction, identifies friction points, switching triggers, and future intent, enabling segmentation based on running intensity, price sensitivity…

targetCustomer.summary: Adult consumers of Running Shoes in U.S. — who Individuals who have bought running shoes in the past 12 months; Individuals who run or exercise regularly (at least once a week); Individuals who are the primary decision-maker for their own shoe purchase. metadata.studyPurpose: Identify which of 4 behavioural segments each respondent belongs to, based on running frequency, purchase drivers, price sensitivity, and sustainability orientation.
metadata.segmentation_lens: Combination of usage/behavioural and price-sensitivity, because running shoes buyers differ fundamentally in how often they run (which drives replacement cycle and performance needs) and how much price constrains their choices (a major pain point in this market).

segments.name: High-Frequency Performance Runners
segments.description: Run multiple times per week, prioritize cushioning, support, and durability, willing to pay premium for performance, replace shoes every 3-6 months.
segments.hypothesis: They will show high spend, low price sensitivity, and strong preference for technical features over style.

segments.name: Price-Sensitive Recreational Runners
segments.description: Run occasionally (1-2 times per week) or for fitness, highly price-conscious, often buy on sale or from discount retailers, value durability and comfort but not willing to pay premium.
segments.hypothesis: They will show low spend, high price sensitivity, and frequent switching based on deals.

segments.name: Eco-Conscious Committed Runners
segments.description: Run regularly and are strongly motivated by sustainability, seek recycled materials and carbon-neutral options, willing to pay more for eco-friendly products, but also expect performance.
segments.hypothesis: They will show moderate-to-high spend, prioritize sustainability claims over brand, and be willing to switch for greener options.

segments.name: Comfort-Led Casual Users
segments.description: Use running shoes for walking, casual wear, or light jogging, prioritize fit and comfort above all, often have foot issues (arch support), less frequent runners, moderate price sensitivity.
segments.hypothesis: They will show lower running frequency, high importance on fit and cushioning, and moderate spend with brand loyalty to comfort-focused brands.

fieldingNotes.recommendedSample: n=800-1,200 for stable segment-level sub-groups (roughly n>=312 per segment after weighting). At n=1,000 the margin of error on a whole-sample percentage is about ±3.1pp at 95% confidence; on a segment of n=200 it widens to about ±6.9pp, so segment-level differences under ~10pp should not be reported as real.
fieldingNotes.quotaControls: Apply quotas on the category-usage and frequency screeners so heavy users — who are more willing survey-takers — are not over-sampled.
scriptingNotes: Rotate the order of answer options on every non-ordinal question to remove primacy bias. Do NOT rotate ordinal scales (frequency bands, price bands, satisfaction) — their order carries meaning.
Anchor 'Other', 'None of these' and 'Prefer not to say' to the bottom of the list, exempt from rotation.
Every 'Other' option takes an open-text capture, coded back into the frame at analysis if any single verbatim exceeds 3%.
No routing or skip logic: every respondent sees every question, so the base is constant across the instrument.
Include one attention check in the middle third — a standard instructed-response item. Terminate on failure and replace.
Randomise the order of the two ranking/trade-off items between respondents so neither is systematically answered while fresher.
caveats: Percentages in this document are modelled from published market evidence, not measured from fielded interviews. Replace them with primary data once the study is run.
Ranking items are shown as a lighter-weight ranking exercise; run them as MaxDiff if you need more precision on driver importance.
Profiling questions are for cross-tabs only and are excluded from the segmentation scoring model.

metadata.storyline_summary: The survey opens by establishing the respondent's running frequency and context, then moves to their shoe ownership and replacement habits, and finally their fit experience. It then traces the purchase journey from trigger through research, channel, and price, ending with the decision drivers. Next, it explores their must-have features, quality cues, sustainability expectations, and trade-offs, closing with value perception. Finally, it measures satisfaction, identifies friction points, switching triggers, and future intent, enabling segmentation based on running intensity, price sensitivity…
storyline_notes: Added a beat on fit and sizing in the consumer profile section because fit is a top pain point in the market and critical for segmentation.
Moved replacement cycle into the consumer profile section as it is a core usage behaviour for running shoes, not just a purchase cycle metric.
Included sustainability credentials as a distinct beat in preferences because of the high environmental awareness in the region and its role in differentiating the Eco-Conscious segment.
Emphasized price paid and decision drivers in the buying behavior section to capture the high price sensitivity noted in the market profile.
The satisfaction section includes switching triggers and future intent to identify potential churn and growth opportunities, aligning with the mixed consumer sentiment.
metadata.classification_reason: Everyday consumers buy running shoes for personal use, pay for them out of pocket, and decide which pair to purchase based on fit, style, and performance. While some businesses may purchase shoes for employees (e.g., athletic teams), the dominant and defining buyer is the individual consumer.
